title: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
summary: How a photo of stars is located on the sky with no first guess: invariant shape codes for star groups, geometric hashing and kd-tree lookup, Bayesian verification, and the resulting WCS.
outcomes: Explain how basis-pair geometric hashing indexes point patterns so they can be found after shift, rotation, scale and occlusion
Compute the Astrometry.net quad code by mapping A to (0,0) and B to (1,1) and show it is unchanged by similarity transforms
Explain why quads beat triangles and quints for blind solving, using code-space oversubscription
Compute a Bayes factor threshold from priors and utilities and trace per-star evidence during verification
Describe how matched stars become a WCS (CRPIX, CRVAL, CD, TAN) and when triangle matching is the better tool

lessons.title: Plate solving: finding where a photo points with no first guess

blocks.md:
You have a photo of the night sky: a few hundred bright dots in pixel coordinates, no header, no idea where the telescope pointed, how it was rotated or how many arcseconds one pixel covers. **Plate solving** (also called *blind astrometric calibration*) recovers exactly those things: the pointing (right ascension and declination), the orientation, and the scale. The output is written as a **WCS** (World Coordinate System) header that maps every pixel to a sky position.

Astronomers call the fully blind version the *lost in space* problem, because an early use was a spacecraft camera working out its own attitude from the stars it sees.

Why is this hard? The answer lives in a continuous four-dimensional space: two numbers for the pointing, one for the rotation, one for the field of view. Lang et al. (2010) wanted to recognize images covering *less than one millionth* of the sky, so trying hypotheses on a grid is hopeless.

Your local-feature-matching toolkit does not help either. SIFT and ORB describe the texture of a small patch around a corner. A star is a point source: every star patch looks like every other star patch, so the descriptors carry almost no identity. The astroalign authors make exactly this point: corner-style features generally fail on stellar images.

blocks.prompt: Stars carry no useful descriptor, so identity must come from *arrangement*. Four stars have 8 pixel coordinates. If you want a description of their shape that ignores where the group sits, how it is rotated and how big it is, how many numbers are left?
blocks.reveal: **Four.** A similarity transform (shift x, shift y, rotation, scale) has 4 degrees of freedom, and 8 minus 4 leaves 4 numbers that describe pure shape. Astrometry.net's hash code for a 4-star *quad* is exactly such a 4-vector. Three stars would leave only 6 minus 4 = 2 numbers, which is why triangle codes are less distinctive.

scenes.caption: Source detection turns pixels into a list of star positions, usually a few hundred, each located to a fraction of a pixel.
Take 4 stars at a time and reduce them to a 4-number hash code that does not change if the image is shifted, rotated or scaled.
Look up all index codes within a small radius. Each one comes from 4 known catalog stars, so each match proposes a full alignment of the image on the sky.
Most proposals are coincidences. Verification asks whether the alignment predicts where the *other* stars in the image are. Rejected proposals send the search back to the next quad.
The first hypothesis that passes a very strict test is returned as a WCS. The thresholds are set so that a false answer is far rarer than no answer.

blocks.md:
This two-stage shape (cheap invariant lookup to propose, expensive check to confirm) is the classic **geometric hashing** recipe from object recognition, which the Astrometry.net paper cites as its basis. Earlier star matchers used the same idea with triangles: Groth (1986) matched triangles between two coordinate lists using the ratio of the longest to shortest side and the cosine of one angle, on the brightest 20 to 30 stars of each list.

This course builds the idea up in order: the general hashing scheme, the quad code, the lookup, the verification test, and finally turning a match into a WCS.

Stars have no texture, so a plate solver identifies them by the *shape* of small groups. The whole design is: describe shape with numbers that ignore position, rotation and scale; look those numbers up; then verify every proposal against the rest of the image.

blocks.question: Why does a SIFT-style detector and descriptor usually fail to plate-solve a star field?
options: SIFT is too slow for images with hundreds of stars
Each star patch looks nearly identical, so the descriptors do not say which star is which
SIFT descriptors change when the image is rotated
SIFT cannot handle images taken at night
blocks.explain: SIFT is rotation and scale invariant, so that is not the issue. The issue is distinctiveness: a star is a point spread function, and one blurred dot looks like another. Identity has to come from the geometric arrangement of several stars.

blocks.question: A plate solver's answer is described by pointing, rotation and field of view. How many continuous numbers is that?
blocks.explain: Pointing on the sky is 2 numbers (RA and Dec), plus 1 rotation angle, plus 1 scale. Lang et al. describe the hypothesis space as continuous and four-dimensional, which is why exhaustive search is impractical.

lessons.title: Geometric hashing: basis pairs, a hash table, and votes

blocks.md:
Geometric hashing comes from model-based object recognition. Lamdan and Wolfson presented it at ICCV 1988 (building on work with Schwartz), and Wolfson and Rigoutsos wrote the standard overview in *IEEE Computational Science and Engineering* (1997). The goal: given a database of point-pattern *models*, find which model appears in a scene, even when it is shifted, rotated, scaled, partly hidden, and mixed with clutter, without comparing the scene to every model one by one.

The trick is to give each point a coordinate that does not depend on the pose. A point's raw (x, y) depends on the frame, so we build the frame *from the points themselves*.

For a similarity transform (shift, rotation, scale), an ordered pair of points is enough to define a frame. Following the overview: put the origin at the midpoint of the pair, point the x axis from the first point to the second, and make the distance between them one unit. Every other point then gets coordinates (u, v) in this frame, and those coordinates are the same in any shifted, rotated or scaled copy of the pattern.

blocks.tex: p - p_0 = u\,\mathbf{p}_x + v\,\mathbf{p}_y,\qquad \mathbf{p}_x = p_{\mu_2} - p_{\mu_1},\quad \mathbf{p}_y = \mathrm{Rot}_{90}(\mathbf{p}_x),\quad p_0 = \tfrac{1}{2}(p_{\mu_1}+p_{\mu_2})
blocks.caption: Equation 1 of Wolfson and Rigoutsos (1997). The basis pair is (p_mu1, p_mu2); u and v are invariant to similarity transforms, and their quantized values (u_q, v_q) are the hash key.

blocks.md:
**Toy model.** Model M1 has five points: p1 (2.9, 2.3), p2 (5.2, 1.8), p3 (4.2, 4.6), p4 (2.0, 5.9), p5 (1.4, 2.7). With basis (p1, p2) the other three points land at p3 (-0.168, 1.072), p4 (-1.199, 1.413), p5 (-1.159, 0.031). We quantize with bins 0.25 wide, so p3 goes to bin key (-1, 4), and we append the entry *(M1, basis (1,2))* to that bin's list.

Because any point might be hidden in a scene, we repeat this for **every ordered pair**: 5 x 4 = 20 bases, each placing 3 points, so 60 entries for M1. A second model M2 adds 60 more.

blocks.title: Hash table occupancy over (u, v) bins of width 0.25

scenes.caption: Basis (p1, p2) of M1 puts its other 3 points into 3 bins. Labels give each bin's lower edge: p3 sits at u = -0.168, v = 1.072.
All 20 ordered bases of M1 give 60 entries. 54 fall inside this window; 6 land farther out (short bases make big u, v). The hash table is a dictionary, so those still exist.
Adding model M2 brings the table to 120 entries (110 shown). Bins start to hold entries from several models; the fullest bin in the whole table holds 5.
Recognition: with scene basis (s1, s2), points s3 and s4 hash to the two highlighted top bins, each holding only (M1, basis (1,2)). The clutter point s5 hits an empty bin (row -0.75, column -0.75).

blocks.md: **Recognition** reverses the process. The scene contains M1 rotated by 50 degrees, scaled by 0.8 and shifted by (10, 5), with p5 hidden and one clutter point added: s1 to s4 are the images of p1 to p4, and s5 is clutter. Pick an ordered pair of scene points as a basis, compute (u, v) for every other scene point, and give one vote to every (model, basis) entry in the bin it hits. A pair that really corresponds to a model basis collects a vote from every visible point of that model.

blocks.title: Votes per (model, basis) for three choices of scene basis

scenes.caption: Scene basis (s1, s2): s3 and s4 both vote for (M1, basis (1,2)). Two votes out of a possible three; the third model point, p5, is hidden.
Scene basis (s3, s4) is also a true correspondence: it gets 2 votes for (M1, basis (3,4)), plus 1 coincidental vote for (M2, basis (5,4)) whose bin happens to be shared.
Scene basis (s1, s5) uses the clutter point, so no model frame matches. None of the 3 other points lands in an occupied bin: zero votes everywhere.

blocks.md:
Votes only *propose*. The overview's final steps recover the transform by least squares over the matched points and check it against the image. Fitting p1 to p4 onto s1 to s4 here recovers scale 0.800, rotation 50.0 degrees and shift (10.0, 5.0), and predicts that p5 should appear at (9.07, 7.25). A verifier would look there; in our scene it is hidden, so the match rests on 4 of 5 points.

The number of points needed for a basis depends on the transformation: 1 for translation only, 2 for similarity (as here), 3 for 2D affine, 4 for 2D projective. Preprocessing costs $O(Mn^{c+1})$ for $M$ models of $n$ points with a $c$-point basis, and recognition costs $O(HS^{c+1})$ for $S$ scene points, where $H$ is the cost of processing one bin.

A hard bin boundary is fragile: noise of a few thousandths can push u from 0.249 to 0.251 and the vote goes to the wrong bin. Practical systems search neighboring bins, or, like Astrometry.net, skip fixed bins and do a radius search in continuous code space.

Geometric hashing moves the expensive work offline: every model is stored under every basis. At query time one correct scene basis is enough, and it never needs to know in advance which model point it corresponds to.

blocks.question: Why does the table store each model under *all* ordered basis pairs rather than just one canonical pair?
options: To make the table smaller
Because the canonical pair might be hidden or missing in the scene, and any visible pair must still be able to find the model
Because a single pair does not define a frame under similarity transforms
To avoid quantization errors at bin edges
blocks.explain: Occlusion and clutter are the whole point. If only basis (p1, p2) were stored and p1 were hidden, the model could never be found. Storing all n(n-1) bases means any two visible model points can serve as the scene basis.

blocks.question: You switch from similarity transforms to full 2D affine transforms (adding shear and non-uniform scale). What changes in the scheme?
options: The basis needs three non-collinear points, so preprocessing grows from O(Mn^3) to O(Mn^4)
Nothing; two points still define the frame
Hashing no longer works and you must compare all models directly
You need a 3D hash table
blocks.explain: Affine maps have 6 degrees of freedom, so 3 points are needed to fix a frame (the overview lists a three-point basis for 2D affine). With c = 3 the preprocessing cost O(Mn^(c+1)) becomes O(Mn^4), and recognition must try ordered triples of scene points.

lessons.title: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step

blocks.md:
Astrometry.net replaces geometric hashing's discrete bins with a continuous 4-number code for a group of four stars, a **quad**. The recipe from Lang et al. (2010):

1. Of the four stars, the most widely separated pair are **A** and **B**.
2. Build a local frame where A is at (0, 0) and B is at (1, 1).
3. The other two stars, **C** and **D**, get coordinates in that frame. The code is $(x_C, y_C, x_D, y_D)$.
4. C and D must lie inside the circle that has A and B on its diameter.

This is the geometric hashing basis-pair idea with one canonical basis (the widest pair) instead of all pairs, and with A at a corner rather than at the midpoint.

blocks.tex: \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \frac{1}{|AB|^2}\begin{pmatrix} AB_x + AB_y & AB_y - AB_x \\ AB_x - AB_y & AB_x + AB_y \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} P_x - A_x \\ P_y - A_y \end{pmatrix}
blocks.caption: The similarity transform used in Astrometry.net's quad_compute_star_code (written here in plain pixel coordinates). It scales by sqrt(2)/|AB| and rotates so that B lands exactly on (1, 1).

blocks.md: **Toy quad** in pixel coordinates: A (300, 180), B (100, 100), C (240, 110), D (170, 180). AB is the longest of the six distances (215.41 px; the next longest is 140.36 px). The circle on diameter AB has center (200, 140) and radius 107.70 px, and both C and D sit 50.0 px from the center, safely inside. Step through the arithmetic:

blocks.title: Computing the quad code for A, B, C, D
blocks.code:
A = (300, 180); B = (100, 100)   # widest pair
C = (240, 110); D = (170, 180)
ABx, ABy = B[0] - A[0], B[1] - A[1]
s = ABx**2 + ABy**2                # squared length of AB
cos_t = (ABx + ABy) / s
sin_t = (ABy - ABx) / s

def frame(P):                      # A goes to (0,0), B to (1,1)
    dx, dy = P[0] - A[0], P[1] - A[1]
    return (dx*cos_t + dy*sin_t, -dx*sin_t + dy*cos_t)

xB, yB = frame(B)
xC, yC = frame(C)
xD, yD = frame(D)
code = (xC, yC, xD, yD)

scenes.caption: The basis vector from A to B.
Its squared length sets the scale: dividing by s shrinks AB to unit-ish size.
These two numbers are not a true cosine and sine; they fold the scale sqrt(2)/|AB| and the 45 degree twist (so B lands on (1,1), not (1,0)) into one matrix.
Sanity check: B itself maps to exactly (1, 1).
The hash code. It also satisfies the symmetry-breaking rules: xC <= xD and xC + xD = 0.9655 <= 1.

blocks.title: The quad in its own frame: A at (0,0), B at (1,1)

scenes.caption: In the local frame A and B are pinned to (0,0) and (1,1). Only C and D carry information: their 4 coordinates are the code.
C and D must fall inside the circle with AB as diameter (center (0.5, 0.5), radius 0.7071). This guarantees AB really is the widest pair and keeps codes in a bounded region.

blocks.prompt: Now rotate the whole photo by 30 degrees, enlarge it by 1.5x and shift it by (400, 50) pixels. A moves to (654.71, 508.83). What happens to the code (0.1810, 0.5776, 0.7845, 0.3362)?
blocks.reveal: **Nothing.** Recomputing from the new pixel positions gives (0.1810, 0.5776, 0.7845, 0.3362) to four decimals. Shifts cancel when we subtract A, and the rotation and scale are absorbed because the frame is built from AB itself. This is the whole reason the code can be precomputed from a catalog and looked up from any photo.

blocks.title: The same quad under different image transformations

scenes.caption: The code (xC, yC, xD, yD) of the toy quad in its original orientation.
Rotated 30 degrees, scaled 1.5x and shifted: identical code. Invariance is exact, not approximate.
Add Gaussian noise (sigma 0.5 px) to each star of the transformed quad: the code moves by a Euclidean distance of 0.0044. Smooth, small changes; this is why lookup is a radius search.
Mirror the image (flip x): with the same labels each (x, y) pair swaps. A similarity transform cannot undo a reflection, so the solver searches the flipped code too.
Calling the other end of the widest pair A gives 1 minus every value. The rule mean(xC, xD) <= 0.5 picks one labeling, and xC <= xD fixes which star is C.

blocks.md:
Two symmetries would otherwise give one quad several codes. Swapping A and B maps the code to $(1-x_C, 1-y_C, 1-x_D, 1-y_D)$; swapping C and D swaps the two pairs. The paper breaks both by requiring $x_C \le x_D$ and $x_C + x_D \le 1$, and the source code enforces the second as the mean of the x values being at most 1/2.

The paper lists three properties that make this code good for indexing: it is invariant to translation, rotation and scale; it is *smooth* (small star motions give small code motions); and if stars are uniform on the sky, codes spread uniformly over the 4D code region.

Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities. Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.
Quad code = coordinates of C and D in the frame where A is (0,0) and B is (1,1). Four numbers, independent of where the quad is, how it is turned, or how big it looks.

blocks.question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
blocks.explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2 > 1 and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

blocks.question: Your star detector has 0.5 px centroid noise. Which statement about the quad code is right?
options: Noise has no effect because the code is invariant
Noise moves the code slightly, by an amount that shrinks as the quad gets larger in pixels
Noise flips the parity of the code
Noise makes the code depend on rotation
blocks.explain: Invariance covers similarity transforms, not independent per-star jitter. Jitter moves C and D relative to A and B; in the unit frame the effect is roughly the noise divided by |AB|, so larger quads give more stable codes. In the toy, 0.5 px noise on a 323 px quad moved the code by 0.0044.

lessons.title: Searching code space: kd-trees, tolerance and why quads beat triangles

blocks.md:
Because noisy stars give slightly different codes, the solver never asks for an *exact* key. It asks for every index code within a distance $r$ of the query code. Astrometry.net stores the codes in a **kd-tree**, a binary tree that splits space along one coordinate at a time, so a radius query only visits the few cells near the query.

The default code tolerance in the source is 0.01. In the paper's SDSS experiment the solver searched within 0.01, which the authors describe as well into the tail of the measured distances between a query quad and its correct index quad.

blocks.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree

def quad_code(A, B, C, D):
    ab = B - A
    s = ab @ ab
    cos, sin = (ab[0] + ab[1]) / s, (ab[1] - ab[0]) / s
    def frame(P):
        d = P - A
        return [d[0]*cos + d[1]*sin, -d[0]*sin + d[1]*cos]
    return np.array(frame(C) + frame(D))

q = quad_code(np.array([300., 180.]), np.array([100., 100.]),
              np.array([240., 110.]), np.array([170., 180.]))
print(q.round(4))                 # [0.181  0.5776 0.7845 0.3362]

codes = np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(0, 1, (100_000, 4))
codes[42] = q + 0.003             # the true match, slightly noisy
tree = cKDTree(codes)
print(tree.query_ball_point(q, r=0.01))   # [42]
blocks.caption: The toy quad looked up among 100,000 random 4D codes with a radius-0.01 kd-tree query. Only the planted true match comes back.

blocks.md:
Every code that comes back is a **hypothesis**: the 4 image stars are these 4 catalog stars. The danger is coincidental neighbors. The paper's term is the **oversubscription** of code space: the number of codes in the index times the fraction of code space each code effectively occupies. If that product is large, every query hits many random codes, and each must be rejected by expensive verification.

In a simplified uniform model, C and D each fall in a disk of area $\pi/2$, the two symmetry rules divide by 4, and a query ball of radius $t$ in 4D has volume $\pi^2 t^4/2$. The fraction is $8t^4$. The analogous triangle code (one free star, one symmetry rule) gives $4t^2$.

blocks.title: Expected chance matches per query (uniform-code toy model)

scenes.caption: At t = 0.01 a quad code covers 8e-8 of code space and a triangle code 4e-4. With a million codes that is 0.08 chance matches per quad query versus 400 per triangle query.
Halve the tolerance: quads drop 16x (t to the 4th), triangles only 4x (t squared). Simplified: real codes are not uniform and the index is split by scale.
Double the tolerance to absorb more noise: quad false matches rise 16x but stay manageable for modest indexes; triangles become hopeless.

blocks.md: This is the paper's argument for quads: a quad is like two triangles sharing an edge, so it nearly squares the distinctiveness. Why not five stars? Two costs: all k stars must be detected in the image *and* present in the catalog, which gets less likely as k grows, and nearest-neighbor search slows in higher dimensions (6D for quints). The paper tested all three on 4000 SDSS images, using tolerances that capture 95% of correct matches (0.0064 for triangles, 0.0095 for quads, 0.011 for quints).

blocks.title: Percent of SDSS test images solved vs CPU time (Lang et al. 2010)

scenes.caption: After 0.1 s of CPU per image, quads have already solved 57.45% of images; triangles 0.20%, drowning in coincidental matches.
After 1 s: quads 92.20%, triangles 28.07%, quints 36.67%. Quints are distinctive but need many quads tried before one is fully present.
After 10 s: quads 99.28%, triangles 78.58%, quints 72.75%.
Final rates (brightest 50 stars): triangles 99.97%, quads 99.33%, quints 96.25%. Triangles eventually find more, but far too slowly.

blocks.md:
**Building the index.** Lang et al. lay an equal-area HEALPix grid over the sky with cells about a third the size of the target images, keep the 10 brightest stars per cell, then try to build one quad per cell whose center lies in the cell and whose diameter is in the chosen range. Stars that have been used too often are skipped, so no single star (which might be missing in a photo) carries too much weight. A typical run makes 16 passes and lets each star join up to 8 quads. The SDSS index held about 100 million stars and 150 million quads, about 5 GB.

To handle images of any size, there is a family of sub-indexes, each covering a narrow range of quad diameters. The current docs list the 4100 and 5200 series (for example, index-5202 covers 4.0 to 5.6 arcmin quads) and suggest using index files whose quads are 10% to 100% of your image size.

Telling solve-field roughly how big the image is (`--scale-low`, `--scale-high`) speeds it up a lot: it skips index files with quads of the wrong size, and rejects matches that would imply an out-of-range scale before running verification.

blocks.question: You double the code-match tolerance to cope with a noisy camera. In the uniform toy model, by what factor do chance matches per query grow for quads?
options: 2x
4x
8x
blocks.explain: The query region is a 4D ball whose volume grows as t to the 4th power, so doubling t multiplies chance matches by 16. For 2D triangle codes it would be 4x. This is why quads tolerate a larger index before verification costs explode.

blocks.question: Why did quint (5-star) indexes solve images more slowly than quads, even though a quint match is almost always correct?
options: 6D kd-tree lookups are impossible
The solver must try many quints before finding one whose 5 stars are all in both the image and the index, and higher-dimensional search is slower
Quint codes are not scale invariant
Quints produce more coincidental matches than triangles
blocks.explain: The paper reports that for over 80% of solved images the first quint match found was correct. The cost is elsewhere: the chance that all 5 stars are detected and catalogued is lower, so many more quints are tried, and near-neighbor search slows with dimension.

lessons.title: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion

blocks.md:
Lookup produces a flood of hypotheses. In the SDSS run, over 180 million quads were tried and they produced about 77 million index matches, for 182,221 images. Many implied an image scale outside the allowed range and were dropped cheaply, so the full verification ran about 6 million times. The verifier's job is to reject almost all of these and accept a true one quickly.

The question it asks: *if this alignment were right, where else in the image should stars be?* A true alignment predicts the positions of dozens of other stars. A coincidental quad match predicts nothing.

Lang et al. frame this as a Bayesian decision between a **foreground** model F (alignment true) and a **background** model B (alignment false). The **Bayes factor** $K = p(D \mid F)/p(D \mid B)$ compares how well each explains the observed star positions D. Two more ingredients set the bar: a prior odds of $10^{-6}$ that any given proposal is correct, and a utility table that makes a false positive cost 1999 times what a correct answer gains.

blocks.caption: Accept when the expected utility of accepting beats rejecting. With the paper's prior and utilities this becomes a Bayes factor threshold of one billion, which matches solve-field's default odds-to-solve of 1e9.

blocks.md: Each image star is scored in brightness order. Under B, a star is equally likely anywhere in the image of area $A$, density $1/A$. Under F, a star is either a *distractor* (no catalog counterpart: an artifact, a planet, a missing catalog entry) spread uniformly, or it sits in a Gaussian blob around one of the $N_R$ catalog stars the alignment predicts in the field. The per-star ratio is multiplied into K, so its log is added.

blocks.caption: Simplified from the paper's description and the verify code. d is the distractor fraction (default 0.25), r the distance to the nearest predicted catalog star, sigma the combined position error.

blocks.md: **Toy numbers.** A 1000 x 1000 px image ($A = 10^6$), $N_R = 50$ predicted catalog stars, $\sigma = 1$ px, $d = 0.25$. A star landing exactly on a prediction scores a ratio of 2387.6 ($\log_{10} = 3.38$); at 1 px off, 1448.2 (3.16); at 3 px, 26.8 (1.43). A star with no prediction nearby scores about 0.25 ($\log_{10} = -0.60$): mild evidence *against*, because F spends 75% of its probability on the blobs.

blocks.title: Running log10 Bayes factor for a true alignment, star by star

scenes.caption: Star 1 lands 0.4 px from a predicted catalog star: log10 K = 3.34.
Star 2 lands 0.7 px from a prediction: +3.27, total 6.61. Already a million to one, but not yet past the 1e9 bar.
Star 3 has no counterpart (maybe a satellite or a defect): it costs 0.60, total 6.01. One distractor does not sink a true match.
Star 4 at 0.3 px: total 9.37, past log10 K = 9. With the default settings the solver can accept here.
More stars keep piling on evidence (12.49, then 15.81). True matches typically reach overwhelming odds; the paper notes that keeping only the 50 brightest SDSS stars would have given similar results.

blocks.md:
A *false* alignment predicts catalog stars at essentially random places. Each image star then usually lands far from all 50 predictions and contributes about $-0.60$; after 6 stars log10 K is about $-3.61$ and falling. How likely is a false alignment to sneak through by luck? Under B the chance that one star lands within $3\sigma$ of any of the 50 predictions is $50 \cdot \pi \cdot 3^2 / 10^6 = 0.0014$. Among the 20 brightest stars:

- at least 1 chance hit: 0.028
- at least 2: 3.7e-4
- at least 3: 3.2e-6
- at least 4: 1.9e-8

Each chance hit is worth roughly 1.4 to 3.4 in log10 K, so a false alignment needs several independent lucky hits to approach 9. The probability falls by roughly a factor of 100 per extra hit.

blocks.prompt: The paper's thresholds give essentially zero false positives on hundreds of thousands of SDSS images. What kind of input image do you think still fools it?
blocks.reveal: Images that break the model's assumption that unmatched stars are scattered at random. The paper's example is a photo crossed by the International Space Station: the streak became a *line* of detected sources, which aligned with a line of false sources detected in the writing on a scanned USNO-B photographic plate. Correlated structure in both image and catalog makes many 'hits' at once, so the independent-hits arithmetic no longer applies.

blocks.md: The verification math assumes stray detections are independent and uniform. Satellite trails, diffraction spikes, plate scratches and dense clusters violate that, so false positives there are far more common than the formula predicts. Mask streaks before solving.

Retrieval is cheap and noisy; verification is strict. Each match is a full alignment that predicts many other stars, and the Bayes factor multiplies independent evidence, so a true match passes 1e9 within a handful of stars while chance matches almost never do.

blocks.question: You lower the prior odds that a proposal is correct from 1e-6 to 1e-8, keeping the utilities. What is the new Bayes factor threshold?
blocks.explain: The threshold is (p(B)/p(F)) times (u(TN) - u(FP))/(u(TP) - u(FN)) = 1e8 x 2000/2 = 1e11. Lower prior belief in any one proposal means more evidence is required before accepting.

blocks.question: During verification, star 3 of a true alignment is a satellite with no catalog counterpart. Why does the foreground model include a distractor term d instead of putting all probability on the predicted catalog stars?
options: Without it, any single unmatched star would give a ratio near zero and could veto a correct alignment
To make the computation faster
Because the background model also has a distractor term
To make the false positive rate exactly zero
blocks.explain: If F gave zero probability to stars away from predictions, one artifact, planet or catalog gap would multiply K by almost zero. The mixture with d = 0.25 caps the penalty at about -0.6 in log10 per stray star, so real images with junk still solve.

lessons.title: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative

blocks.md:
An accepted hypothesis pairs image stars with catalog stars. To publish it, the solver fits a mapping from pixels to the sky and writes it in the FITS **WCS** convention (Greisen and Calabretta 2002; Calabretta and Greisen 2002). The core chain for a simple solution:

1. Subtract the reference pixel **CRPIX**.
2. Multiply by the 2 x 2 **CD** matrix (degrees per pixel, including rotation) to get *intermediate world coordinates* (x, y).
3. Deproject (x, y) onto the sphere around the reference sky position **CRVAL** using a projection named in CTYPE, typically **TAN** (gnomonic) for optical cameras.

blocks.tex: \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{CD}\begin{pmatrix} p_1 - r_1 \\ p_2 - r_2 \end{pmatrix},\qquad R_\theta = \frac{180^\circ}{\pi}\cot\theta \;\;(\text{TAN})
blocks.caption: Pixel p, reference pixel r (CRPIX). The TAN projection relates the radial distance in the (x, y) plane to the native latitude theta; theta = 90 degrees at the reference point.

blocks.title: How a WCS turns a pixel into a sky position

scenes.caption: Reading a WCS: subtract the reference pixel, apply the linear CD matrix, then project onto the sky.
Solving a WCS runs the other way: the matched star pairs determine the CD matrix and the sky position of the reference point.
Simplified: Astrometry.net then fine-tunes the fit with more matched stars and by default adds SIP polynomial distortion terms on top of TAN.

blocks.md: **Toy fit.** Suppose the matched catalog stars for our quad A, B, C, D have tangent-plane positions (in arcsec, relative to the field center) of (-91.8, -749.3), (-386.9, -1063.2), (-141.7, -926.7) and (-327.9, -859.0), with about 0.1 arcsec catalog noise. A least-squares similarity fit (4 unknowns from 8 equations) gives scale **2.000 arcsec/px**, rotation **24.98 degrees**, rms residual 0.12 arcsec per coordinate, and maps the image center pixel (500, 500) to within 0.4 arcsec of the field center. As a CD matrix in degrees per pixel:

blocks.caption: Toy numbers computed with numpy. Mirroring the image flips the sign of det CD, one reason the solver tracks parity.

blocks.md:
**The triangle alternative.** When you already have two images of overlapping sky (not an image and an all-sky catalog), the search is far smaller, and triangles work well. Groth (1986) matched all triangles among about 20 to 30 bright stars per list, then removed false matches by noting that true matches share one magnification: the log of the perimeter ratio clusters for true matches and scatters for false ones. Groth estimated the total work grows as about $n^{4.5}$.

[astroalign](https://github.com/quatrope/astroalign) (Beroiz, Cabral and Sanchez 2020) is a modern version: for each bright star it forms the 10 triangles among the star and its 4 nearest neighbors, describes each by side ratios $(L_2/L_1, L_1/L_0)$, matches them with kd-trees, and fits the transform with RANSAC, accepting it when it fits 80% of the remaining points (or 10, whichever is smaller).

From the paper's discussion: star trackers use triangles because their fields span tens of degrees with only dozens of bright stars. Lang et al. expect triangle indexes to win for images much larger than SDSS fields and quint indexes for much smaller ones; quads were best at SDSS size.
A match is not the end product. The solver turns matched star pairs into CRPIX, CRVAL and a CD matrix under a TAN projection, which any FITS tool can then use to label every pixel with RA and Dec.

blocks.question: You have hundreds of frames of the same field from one night and want to stack them. Which approach fits best?
options: Blind-solve each frame against an all-sky quad index, every time
Use SIFT descriptors on the star patches
Register frames to each other with triangle asterism matching (as in astroalign), solving just one frame blind if you need sky coordinates
Assume the frames are already aligned
blocks.explain: Frame-to-frame registration has a tiny search space, where triangle matching plus RANSAC is fast and reliable. Blind all-sky solving is for when you do not know where the image points; doing it per frame is wasteful.

blocks.question: A solved WCS has CD matrix entries giving sqrt(|det CD|) = 0.000556 degrees per pixel. What is the pixel scale in arcseconds?
options: 0.556 arcsec/px
33.4 arcsec/px
0.0333 arcsec/px
2.0 arcsec/px
blocks.explain: One degree is 3600 arcsec, so 0.000556 x 3600 = 2.0 arcsec per pixel. The square root of the determinant removes the rotation and leaves the linear scale.

blocks.question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
blocks.explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.
